section_summary: This section documents State Department, War Department, Navy Department, and FBI inquiries during 1940–1941 into allegations that Japanese consular officials and Japanese associations were registering or recruiting Japanese Americans for service in Japan. Early investigations found little evidence that exclusively American citizens were being conscripted, although dual nationals were required to report their military status and apply annually for deferment; later FBI investigations found that Japanese associations collected military-age information for the Japanese Consulate and transferred funds connected with Japan. The section also contains conscription notices and forms, correspondence concerning dual citizenship, telegrams about Russian émigré mobilization in North China, and competing public claims by the Sino-Korean Peoples’ League and the Japanese American Citizens League.

subfiles.title: Sino-Korean Peoples’ League complaint concerning Japanese registration in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.about: Alleges that Japanese consular officials are registering dual-national Japanese Americans in Hawaii for Japanese military service.
subfiles.summary: Haan asks the State Department to halt the reported registration of Japanese males aged 21–36 and obtain the registrants’ names. He links the activity to the recent Japanese census and cites public objections by Senator William H. King and Representative Fred L. Crawford as evidence of the perceived danger to national defense.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Haan’s complaint to the Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards a photostatic copy of Haan’s December 17 complaint for confidential FBI use.
subfiles.summary: The Department transmits the Sino-Korean Peoples’ League letter in the hope that its allegations will be useful to the FBI. The enclosure is identified as a photostatic copy of Haan’s December 17, 1940 letter.

subfiles.title: Instruction enclosing the State Department reply concerning alleged conscription
subfiles.about: Sends the ambassador a confidential copy of the Department’s reply to Senator Gillette.
subfiles.summary: The instruction describes complaints that Japan was conscripting American citizens of Japanese ancestry in Hawaii and on the mainland. It encloses the January 8 reply sent to Senator Guy M. Gillette.

subfiles.title: Senator Gillette’s inquiry concerning Japanese conscription allegations
subfiles.about: Requests information on verification and official action concerning the Sino-Korean Peoples’ League complaint.
subfiles.summary: Gillette reports that representatives of the League filed allegations of current conscription in Hawaii and on the mainland. He asks whether the Department has verified the claims and what action has been taken, emphasizing Hawaii’s strategic and racial-security implications.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Gillette
subfiles.about: Explains the Department’s preliminary findings and the law affecting dual nationals who enter foreign military service.
subfiles.summary: The Department says it has no evidence that Japanese agents are conscripting people in American territory and suggests the reports may stem from census-registration circulars. It distinguishes lawful consular registration from prohibited enlistment under Title 18 and explains that serving in a foreign armed force could cause loss of American nationality under the Nationality Act of 1940. It also notes expatriation presumptions applicable to some dual nationals residing abroad.

subfiles.title: Request to the Navy Department for information
subfiles.about: Asks the Navy Department for pertinent information concerning alleged Japanese conscription in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The Department encloses Gillette’s letter, its reply, and Haan’s original complaint. It requests any existing Navy information or appropriately obtainable investigative findings.

subfiles.title: Request to the Department of Justice for information
subfiles.about: Asks the Justice Department to investigate alleged Japanese conscription of American citizens.
subfiles.summary: The letter encloses the Gillette correspondence and Haan complaint. It requests pertinent information already held by Justice or obtainable through an appropriate investigation.

subfiles.title: Request to the War Department for information
subfiles.about: Requests War Department information about alleged Japanese conscription in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends copies of the Gillette and Haan correspondence. It asks the War Department to report relevant information in its possession or developed through investigation.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs assessment of Haan’s January 4 letter
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Concludes that the quoted Tokyo Gazette language does not connect census registration to military conscription.
subfiles.summary: The brief note finds nothing substantially new in Haan’s latest submission. It states that the Tokyo Gazette quotation does not establish that census registration was related to conscription.

subfiles.title: Sino-Korean Peoples’ League follow-up concerning registration
subfiles.about: Argues that Japanese registration of dual citizens is itself a military and internationally improper act.
subfiles.summary: Haan reports Acting Consul General Otojiro Okuda’s admission that Japanese subjects and dual citizens were being registered, though Okuda denied they would be called while remaining in Hawaii. Haan contrasts Okuda’s denial of military significance with a Tokyo Gazette statement describing the census as part of strengthening Japan’s total-war structure.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning Shiow Yamamoto and expatriation
subfiles.about: References a Hawaiian federal-court decision on whether a native Hawaiian lost citizenship through Japanese Army service.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that a United States District Court judge in Hawaii ruled that an allegiance pledge associated with compulsory Japanese military training did not by itself demonstrate an oath producing expatriation. It directs the reader to the original September 25, 1940 court document concerning Yamamoto.

subfiles.title: War Department acknowledgment of the conscription inquiry
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the State Department request and promises a later report.
subfiles.summary: Stimson confirms receipt of the January 8 letter and its enclosures. He says the matter is receiving attention and that further information will be supplied.

subfiles.title: FBI acknowledgment and announcement of further investigation
subfiles.about: Reports that current evidence concerns Japanese nationals or dual citizens and orders further investigation of exclusively American citizens.
subfiles.summary: Hoover recalls an earlier FBI finding that census questionnaires had not been shown to have gone beyond Japanese nationals and dual nationals. He says additional investigation will determine whether American citizens without Japanese nationality were being conscripted.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on preliminary FBI reports
subfiles.about: Finds the FBI evidence on recruitment and fundraising inconclusive and recommends continued investigation.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to attached FBI reports about recruiting Japanese residents for military service and collecting funds from them. It considers the information received so far inconclusive and favors continuation of the FBI inquiry.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter transmitting investigative data
subfiles.about: Forwards FBI data that may interest the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Hoover provides the enclosed investigative material without substantive comment in the cover letter. The enclosure concerns the alleged Japanese Protective Association and recruitment for the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: FBI report on the Japanese Protective Association and enlistment in the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: Investigates allegations that a San Diego Japanese organization recruited young men for Japanese Army service and collected a head tax.
subfiles.summary: The report records Harlan Page Perrill’s and Jean Morishita’s claims that George Morishita had been urged to go to Japan, although Jean could not identify the recruiters and later became reluctant to cooperate. It also reports that K. Hashimoto accompanied about forty young men to Japan, ostensibly for kendo training, and reviews Montgomery Godley’s claim that Japanese residents were assessed a head tax. The report assigns investigative leads in Washington, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and San Diego to determine whether foreign-agent-registration or neutrality laws were violated.

subfiles.title: State Department response concerning foreign-agent registration
subfiles.about: States that the Japanese Protective Association was not registered as an agent of a foreign principal.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Hoover’s transmittal of Gilliam’s San Diego report. Responding to an investigative lead, it confirms that the Japanese Protective Association had not registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

subfiles.title: War Department findings on Japanese conscription abroad
subfiles.about: Reports no evidence of active Japanese-government conscription of American citizens in Hawaii or on the mainland.
subfiles.summary: The War Department says Japan did not appear eager to use overseas nationals, partly because they were thought unable to subsist on Japanese field rations. Japanese subjects abroad nevertheless had to register, and those who failed to file annual exemption applications could eventually be conscripted, sometimes under family pressure. The Department found no evidence that Japan was actively conscripting American citizens of Japanese parentage.

subfiles.title: Summary of replies to State Department conscription inquiries
subfiles.about: Summarizes the FBI, War Department, and Navy Department responses and advises against volunteering the findings to Senator Gillette.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes the continuing FBI inquiry and recounts War and Navy conclusions that Japan had not actively pressed conscription of American citizens. It explains the registration and annual-deferment procedure for Japanese nationals abroad. It recommends withholding the reassuring findings unless Gillette asks again, lest Japan infer that the United States was unconcerned.

subfiles.title: Navy Department report on Japanese military-service postponements
subfiles.from: Frank Knox, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Describes annual postponement applications by Japanese male nationals residing in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The Navy reports no evidence of actual conscription in the United States. It says Japanese male nationals, generally aged 18–42, presented themselves to Japanese Association offices during the December-to-February registration period and were normally assured postponement before their applications went to the nearest consulate.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on the San Diego FBI inquiry
subfiles.from: Coville, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Notes that the FBI found no confirmation of Japanese Army recruiting in the San Diego area.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum calls attention to the attached San Diego FBI findings. Those findings indicated that there was no substantiated recruiting of Japanese boys for service in Japan.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter transmitting San Diego data
subfiles.about: Transmits additional FBI investigative material.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards data considered potentially useful to the State Department. The enclosure reports the San Diego investigation of the purported Japanese Protective Association.

subfiles.title: FBI follow-up report on the Japanese Protective Association
subfiles.about: Reports that no organization of the stated name or recruitment program could be verified in San Diego County.
subfiles.summary: Confidential informants said they had never heard of a specific Japanese Protective Association or of local boys being recruited for the Japanese Army. The report nevertheless records a Japanese-language notice requiring Japanese nationals of conscription age to register and submit deferment requests. The case remained pending despite the negative local findings.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter transmitting Honolulu communications
subfiles.about: Forwards communications concerning the Honolulu conscription inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends additional material for Berle’s information. The following report concerns Kiyoshi Kurisu and Japanese consular handling of his military summons.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Kiyoshi Kurisu and the Japanese Consulate in Honolulu
subfiles.about: Examines Kurisu’s reports, Japanese military summons, and conversation with a consular employee.
subfiles.summary: Kurisu said he did not remember filing most conscription forms, though his father may have submitted a residence-verification form for him. Katsukichi Muraoka told him it was his duty to return to Japan but admitted the consulate could not force him, and asked that the incident not be discussed. Kurisu refused to return, surrendered a receipt coupon to the consulate, and showed that he had registered for United States selective service in Honolulu.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter transmitting a San Diego follow-up report
subfiles.about: Forwards another FBI report on the alleged recruitment case.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends the enclosed data without further analysis. The enclosure concerns interviews with members of the Morishita family.

subfiles.title: FBI report on the Morishita family’s denial of recruitment
subfiles.about: Records denials that George Morishita had been approached to serve in the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: After repeated attempts, agents located Ruth Morishita and her mother in Spring Valley. Both denied knowledge that anyone had tried to persuade George Morishita to go to Japan and said they would have known if such an approach had occurred.

subfiles.title: American Loyalty League letter on expatriation from Japanese citizenship
subfiles.from: Joseph D. Sasaki, American Loyalty League
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese American Citizens League efforts to promote expatriation from Japanese nationality.
subfiles.summary: Sasaki says the JACL printed one thousand expatriation petitions and was pursuing a sustained expatriation campaign. He explains that Japanese property interests inherited through family relations complicated the process and estimated that settlement and expatriation could require at least nine months.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Joseph D. Sasaki
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Sasaki’s additional information about Japanese American dual citizenship.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton assures Sasaki that the Department will give appropriate consideration to the information. The reply does not make a substantive commitment concerning expatriation policy.

subfiles.title: FBI findings concerning exclusively American and dual-national Japanese Americans
subfiles.about: Reports no known effort to register exclusively American citizens but describes pressures on dual-national Nisei.
subfiles.summary: Los Angeles sources knew of no exclusively American Japanese person asked to register or serve, although they had heard of dual nationals going to Japan. Haan likewise offered no specific case involving exclusive American citizenship but said some Nisei unknowingly possessed Japanese nationality and could be pressured by parents and the community. He also claimed that purported visits or medical examinations could place them under Japanese jurisdiction and lead to forced military service.

subfiles.title: Peiping telegram on mobilization of Russian émigrés
subfiles.from: Butrick, for the American Ambassador at Peiping
subfiles.about: Advises against intervention in Russian émigré mobilization unless American firms are discriminated against.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports similar mobilizations in Peiping and other North China cities. It sees no basis for American intervention unless the Tsingtao action discriminates against American businesses or penalizes them for refusing to pay mobilized employees.

subfiles.title: Tsingtao telegram requesting guidance on Russian émigré mobilization
subfiles.about: Asks whether American authorities should intervene over the mobilization of employees of American firms.
subfiles.summary: About fifty Russian émigrés aged 17–40 were reportedly ordered to intensive training at Tientsin. Two American firms lost essential employees and were told to continue paying their salaries, prompting a request for Embassy inquiries at Peiping.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese conscription in Hawaii
subfiles.about: Points to a Justice Department document about Japanese Consulate assistance with conscription procedures in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies its subject as Japanese conscription in the Territory of Hawaii and consular activities facilitating it. It directs the reader to an October 6, 1941 Justice Department document in another file.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter transmitting conscription investigation reports
subfiles.about: Forwards communications concerning the investigation of Japanese-American conscription allegations.
subfiles.summary: Hoover attaches material deemed potentially useful to the State Department. The following enclosure summarizes investigative work in several California communities.

subfiles.title: FBI report on conscription of American-born Japanese in California
subfiles.about: Surveys reports from several California communities about attempts to induce Japanese Americans to serve in Japan.
subfiles.summary: A San Jose informant described a consular speech, a subsequent sign-up movement, and pressure on American-born Japanese, but later supplied no corroboration. Sources in Sacramento, Modesto, Stockton, San Francisco, and elsewhere generally knew of no direct Japanese-government recruiting in the United States, though they believed military-age visitors to Japan might be inducted. A Hollister informant said the Wada brothers had received letters asking them to return for military service, but had not seen the letters personally.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence transmittal of conscription material
subfiles.about: Forwards two intelligence enclosures, including a translation of a Hawaii Hochi conscription announcement.
subfiles.summary: Miles sends the enclosures for information and any action Berle considers advisable. The relevant enclosure is an October 24 summary and translation concerning Japanese conscription procedures in Hawaii, accompanied by a Japanese-language photostat.

subfiles.title: Translation of Hawaii Hochi announcement and Japanese conscription forms
subfiles.doc_type: intelligence report with translation and photostat
subfiles.to: FBI, Office of Naval Intelligence, and Department of State
subfiles.about: Translates a Japanese consular announcement detailing reporting and deferment requirements for Japanese citizens in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The announcement orders family heads to report males born from December 2, 1921 through December 1, 1922 and warns that delayed reporting violates conscription law. Men abroad were to apply personally for deferment, while earlier cohorts had to renew residence reports. The report reproduces Forms A, B, and C, requesting identity, residence, occupation, special skills, schooling, and deferment information, together with a military-age table and a Japanese-language photostat.

subfiles.title: FBI letter summarizing a New World Sun conscription notice
subfiles.about: Summarizes published procedures for 1942 Japanese conscription reporting and deferment in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The notice required family heads to report men reaching conscription age, required men abroad to seek deferment, and directed older deferred men to submit residence reports. It said Japanese associations or temporary government clerks would distribute the forms and urged correction of unregistered legal residences. Copies were also sent to naval and military intelligence chiefs.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter transmitting a Los Angeles investigation memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum on the Central Japanese Association and related activities in Los Angeles.
subfiles.summary: Hoover says the enclosure outlines recent FBI investigation of aspects of the Japanese situation in Los Angeles. He notes that substantial additional investigation remains and promises a later report.

subfiles.title: Fragment of FBI memorandum on Central Japanese Association records
subfiles.about: Reports findings from translated association records concerning military-age data and financial transfers.
subfiles.summary: The surviving second page says translated records substantiated an informant’s allegations concerning Japanese residents of military age. It identifies approximately $2,700 transferred from the Japanese Consulate to the Central Japanese Association and records additional collections sent to Japan. The material was being correlated for the United States Attorney in Los Angeles.

subfiles.title: Duplicate FBI letter summarizing a New World Sun conscription notice
subfiles.about: Duplicates the summary of published Japanese conscription and deferment procedures.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate describes mandatory reporting for men born in specified age cohorts, applications for deferment by men abroad, and residence reports by previously deferred men. It also identifies Japanese associations as distributors and collection points for the required forms.

subfiles.title: Duplicate FBI transmittal of Los Angeles investigation memorandum
subfiles.about: Duplicates Hoover’s cover letter forwarding the Los Angeles investigation memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Hoover again describes the enclosed memorandum as an outline of recent investigation into the Japanese situation in Los Angeles. He says further investigative work is still required.

subfiles.title: FBI memorandum on the Central Japanese Association and Japanese Chamber of Commerce
subfiles.about: Describes the acquisition and examination of Los Angeles Japanese-association records for possible foreign-agent violations.
subfiles.summary: An informant alleged that the Central Japanese Association and Japanese Chamber of Commerce collected personal data on military-age Japanese men for transmission through the consulate to Japanese military authorities. With authorization from the United States Attorney, agents sought the organizations’ records, which officers voluntarily supplied. Translated records substantiated the data-gathering allegation, showed about $2,700 in consular payments, and documented other funds sent to Japan; prosecutors were to decide what action to take.

subfiles.title: Sino-Korean Peoples’ League press release on the Japanese Military Servicemen’s League
subfiles.about: Claims that Togo Tanaka admitted the existence and dissolution of a Japanese Military Servicemen’s League.
subfiles.summary: The release contrasts Tanaka’s alleged admission with denials by Consuls General Kenji Nakauchi and Nagao Kita. It repeats Senator Gillette’s allegations that the organization had 7,200 members, sent funds to Japan, maintained numerous branches, and influenced the Japanese American Citizens League.

subfiles.title: Translation of Rafu Shimpo notice on military conscription procedure
subfiles.to: Japanese residents of the Los Angeles area
subfiles.about: Announces that the Japanese Association will assist residents with military-age, deferment, and residence reports.
subfiles.summary: The notice directs affected persons to association president Saburo Murayo and secretary Shizuoka. It specifies the birth cohorts required to report military age, request out-of-Empire deferment, or renew residence reports. Haan adds a handwritten accusation that the Los Angeles consulate was using the association to perform consular work.

subfiles.title: Hawaii Hochi conscription announcement presented by Kilsoo Haan
subfiles.from: Hawaii Hochi; presented by Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.about: Reproduces the Honolulu consulate’s instructions for military-age reporting and deferment by Japanese citizens.
subfiles.summary: The announcement requires family heads to report Japanese citizens born in the 1921–1922 cohort and requires affected men to file deferment applications between December 1, 1941 and January 31, 1942. It also lists annual residence-report cohorts and medical qualifications. Haan’s note criticizes Delegate Samuel W. King and editor Riley H. Allen for denying or overlooking consular activity.

subfiles.title: Newspaper clippings on JACL denial of Senator Gillette’s charges
subfiles.from: Unidentified Japanese American newspapers, including material associated with the Hawaii Nippu Jiji and Rafu Shimpo
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese American Citizens League’s denial of subversion allegations and demand for a congressional investigation.
subfiles.summary: Mike Masaoka denies that the JACL was affiliated with Japanese military or comradeship organizations, sold Japanese war bonds, distributed propaganda, or raised money for Japan. The League sent denials to senior federal officials, senators, news organizations, and Senator Gillette, while calling for a separate investigation of itself and of alleged alien propaganda. The clipping also discusses accusations supplied by Kilsoo Haan, his alleged alias Kenneth Maida, and the role of information published in Doho.
